abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel variational framework for image reconstruction based on optimal transport theory, fundamentally departing from conventional L^p norm-based regularization approaches. Traditional image processing methods typically rely on pixel-wise comparisons or patch-based metrics, which fail to capture the underlying geometric structure of image spaces. We propose modeling the image reconstruction problem as an optimal transport problem between probability distributions, enabling a more principled quantification of mass transport during reconstruction. The proposed framework introduces a Wasserstein-based regularization functional that naturally accounts for the metric structure of image manifolds while preserving edges and salient features. We establish well-posedness results demonstrating existence and uniqueness of minimizers in appropriate Banach spaces, and prove convergence guarantees under standard compactness assumptions. Furthermore, we develop a primal-dual algorithm with provable convergence rates for solving the resulting optimization problem. Our theoretical analysis reveals fundamental connections between optimal transport-based imaging and information theory, suggesting that this paradigm shift enables principled handling of illumination variations and geometric deformations. Numerical experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior performance in handling challenging inverse problems, including deblurring, inpainting, and computed tomography reconstruction, validating the practical implications of this theoretical contribution.

This paper presents a rigorous theoretical analysis of plug-and-play (PnP) alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithms for image restoration, addressing a critical gap in the convergence theory of these widely-used methods. While PnP-ADMM has demonstrated remarkable empirical success by integrating denoising priors into iterative optimization, existing convergence analyses rely on restrictive assumptions that rarely hold in practice. We establish novel convergence guarantees under mild conditions satisfied by practical denoisers including Gaussian mixture models and deep neural network-based priors. Our main theoretical contribution is proving that the PnP-ADMM iteration sequence converges to a fixed point of the forward-backward operator, with explicit convergence rates depending on the Lipschitz constant of the denoising operator. We further derive novel error bounds quantifying the distance between the fixed point and the true solution in terms of the noise level and prior quality. A key innovation is introducing the concept of approximate operator resolvent, which enables analysis of denoisers that do not possess firm nonexpansivity properties. These results significantly extend the theoretical understanding of regularization-by-denoising approaches and provide guidance for choosing algorithmic parameters. Our analysis also yields an adaptive stopping criterion that balances data fidelity and prior enforcement, with convergence rates that improve upon existing bounds by a factor related to the condition number of the imaging operator.

We introduce a novel computational imaging framework that integrates physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) with iterative optimization for solving ill-posed inverse problems, representing a fundamental shift from traditional model-based or learning-based approaches. Conventional methods either rely on handcrafted regularization priors or require large annotated datasets for training, limiting their adaptability to novel imaging modalities. Our framework embeds the forward physics model directly into the neural network architecture, enabling the network to learn data-consistent solutions while respecting physical constraints. The proposed architecture employs a learned regularizer implemented as a neural network trained on a physics-motivated manifold, combined with an end-to-end differentiable forward operator that enables gradient-based optimization. We design a multi-resolution training strategy that progressively refines solution quality across scales, addressing the challenge of capturing both global structure and fine details. The system includes a learned projection operator that ensures solution feasibility with respect to the measurement physics. For computed tomography reconstruction, we demonstrate that our approach achieves superior quality with fewer projections than filtered back-projection, fundamentally changing the trade-off between radiation dose and image quality. The framework naturally extends to various imaging modalities including magnetic resonance imaging and electron microscopy, demonstrating its versatility as a new paradigm for computational imaging.

This paper presents a highly efficient multi-scale algorithm for computational imaging that significantly improves reconstruction speed and quality compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Existing approaches to large-scale inverse problems in imaging typically suffer from either excessive computational cost at high resolutions or artifacts arising from hierarchical processing. We propose a novel multi-scale optimization framework that exploits the intrinsic structure of imaging operators through a carefully designed coarse-to-fine strategy with learned transfer operators between scales. The core algorithmic innovation involves a adaptive preconditioning scheme that accelerates convergence while preserving fine image details, combined with a selective update strategy that concentrates computational effort on regions requiring refinement. Our implementation leverages GPU acceleration and sparse matrix operations to achieve real-time reconstruction for images up to 16 megapixels. We introduce a quality metric that automatically detects convergence at each scale, enabling optimal early stopping and preventing over-smoothing. Extensive evaluation on medical imaging tasks including CT reconstruction from sparse views and MRI reconstruction from undersampled k-space data demonstrates that the proposed method achieves 3-5x speedup over current approaches while maintaining or improving reconstruction quality. The algorithm exhibits robust performance across varying noise levels and reconstruction scenarios, with particular improvements in preserving small anatomical structures and low-contrast features essential for diagnostic accuracy.
